cultural.vision_reason: This is a hand-woven indigo strip-cloth gown (riga/boubou/tobe) with large hand-embroidered motifs at the chest and pocket — a garment type long made and worn by Hausa, Nupe and neighbouring peoples of northern Nigeria, so it is consistent with the Nupe attribution even though the exact style cannot distinguish these related groups.

physical.title: gown; textile; tobe
physical.summary: Man’s gown (boubou, tobe, riga). The body is formed of 161 uniform strips, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvedges; the strips are uniform and use indigo-dyed cotton in both warp and weft, with lines of white cotton inserted frequently and regularly in both warp and weft to create a checked appearance of a blue/grey colour (known as ‘saki’ by the Hausa’ and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba). The body of the cloth is not shaped, while the sleeves are wider at the top than the bottom and as a result fan out. At the front is sewn a large pocket. The pocket, shoulder and front are hand-embroidered in white European cotton in a very large rectangle that extends beyond the pocket. The embroidery is in chain and buttonhole eyelet stitch, and in the ‘eight knives’ (aska takwas) pattern; there is a large spiral at the front and another on the back. The knives themselves are embroidered on top of extra pieces of cloth that have been cut to shape. The tunic is unlined and unhemmed except around the neck and sleeves.

physical.title: shirt; tunic
physical.summary: Tunic or shirt tailored from 4 inch wide strips of cotton hand-spun and hand-sewn together. The strips are all of the same composition, using indigo-dyed thread through which lines of white thread have been run in both the warp and the weft. This creates the checkered ‘guinea-fowl’ pattern called ‘saki’ by the Hausa, and ‘etu’ by the Yoruba. The garment is slit down each side to provide openings for the arms, and the openings along the sides and the neck are edged with red cotton. The tunic has been partly lined on the inside with 2 inch strips of hand-spun cotton, which has turned to a shade of blue apparently through contact with the indigo on the front of the tunic. The bottom and sides of the tunic have been hemmed by hand.

cultural.vision_reason: The image shows a hand-woven strip-woven cotton skirt cloth with magenta (alaari silk) and indigo stripes, a traditional Nupe woman's garment construction technique well documented for this people.

physical.title: textile; skirt
physical.summary: Woman’s skirt composed of 22 narrow strips with two warp-faced patterns, hand-woven and hand-sewn together along the selvages; in addition there is a longer edging strip at the top of indigo-dyed cotton thread (with no patterning) which serves as a tie. All the thread is handspun. 19 of the strips have the same pattern, with a central band of magenta silk (alaari) thread flanked by two narrower bands of indigo-dyed cotto, and with two stripes of six threads of white cotton down the centre of the magenta band, while two threads of cotton separate the magenta from the indigo. The remaining 3 strips have a wide band of alaari silk and a narrow band of indigo, but no band of white cotton; these strips form a wide band of silk in the centre and another along the bottom edge, in such a way as to imitate a two-panel cloth of woman’s weave. The weft is of indigo, and the cloth has not been hemmed.

cultural.vision_reason: This is a classic riga/tobe strip-woven and embroidered gown, the type of prestige garment made and worn across the Hausa-Nupe-Yoruba region of Nigeria; the deep pocket and dagger/knot embroidery motifs are consistent with Nupe or closely related Nigerian weaving traditions.

physical.title: gown; tobe
physical.summary: Gown (rigai): oblong shaped body with very broad flared sleeves. Composed of 182 narrow strip plain woven lengths of light and dyed dark blue coloured cotton warps and wefts hand sewn together selvedge to selvedge. There is also evidence that a multicoloured narrow strip/strips were at some point sewn to the bottom of the gown: only tufts remain. The combination of warps and wefts is used to create a blue/grey tunic. There is a large long oblong pocket covering almost 50% of the front body panel.  The tunic is then decorated with extensive embroidery and cutwork using bleached white cotton. The patterns are geometric in shape and arrangement and can be found around the neck extending to a large spiral on the back of the tunic and covering the entire front pocket and across the chest. The tunic is hemmed around the neck and sleeves. Openwork.
